articleTitle: Side-scan sonar records showing thin-film interference patterns in deep-sea sediments
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: In 1986 a GLORIA (6.5 kHz) side-scan sonar survey from 4500m in the Bering Sea revealed an unexplained pattern of backscattering that was sub-parallel to track and similar to the pattern generated by the Lloyds mirror effect. In 1987 part of the previous years survey was repeated and the pattern reappeared in an almost identical fashion. It was concluded that the seafloor sediments were responsible. Since then the pattern has been observed on sediments from many of the world's oceans, and on sonographs from the Institute of Oceanographic Sciences deep towed side-scan (TOBI) which operates at 30 kHz. Several geometries have been considered for the formation of these interference fringes and those in the GLORIA experiments can be attributed to a layer of thickness 3-5 m, the nature of which is a subject of speculation. The implications of these fringes for sonar operators are briefly discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: TOBI is an experimental deep-towed sonar system developed by the Institute of Oceanographic Sciences Deacon Laboratory primarily for investigation of the ocean floor and its underlying structure. The following aspects of the system are discussed: two-bodied tow system; transducer arrays; sonar electronics; telemetry; data logging and display; replay system; and underwater vehicle handling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of air-acoustic sonar systems to advanced manufacturing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: The authors have studied fabrication methods for appropriate electrostatic transducers for such applications as non-contact gauging, workspace imaging and autonomous guided vehicle (AGV) navigation. The following topics are discussed: transducer development; single axis rangefinding; phased array systems for vehicle guidance; phased array systems for workspace imaging; adaptive beamforming; and transmission line matrix modelling of acoustic propagation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High performance signal acquisition systems for sonar applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: Examines the technology/complexity balance in high performance sonar data acquisition systems and describes the development of signal conditioning and A-to-D convertor systems using multi-loop, oversampled sigma-delta convertor techniques, and low complexity digital combiners and recursive interpolators. Various realisations of the basic circuit have been developed for a number of particular applications, using mixtures of thick film, surface mount and VLSI ASIC technologies. It is demonstrated that low cost signal acquisition systems, with dynamic ranges up to 120 dB and power per sensor requirements of the order of a few milliwatts, can be routinely produced on available technologies using these techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Acoustic Doppler current profiler-a sonar system to estimate currents and scattering
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: The acoustic doppler current profiler (ADCP) is standard equipment on many oceanographic research vessels. The sonar estimates the current using the Doppler shift of echoes from zooplankton present in the upper ocean. With the assumption that the targets are drifting with the current, and knowing the absolute velocity of the ship using the GPS satellite navigation system, profiles of the absolute current in the upper 300-500m of the ocean can be made routinely. A by-product of the current measurement is the strength of the backscattered signal, which forms the basis for the zooplankton abundance estimate. The data, which are digitally logged, are processed using shipboard computers to produce sections and maps of currents and scattering. Careful calibration is needed before scattering signal can be related to biomass. As examples of the use of shipboard ADCPs data are given for ocean current monitoring in the region of the Iceland Faeroes in July-August 1990 and for zooplankton abundance estimation in the region of the Indian Ocean atoll of Aldabra in 1987.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Civil Applications of Sonar Systems
abstract: The sonar enhancement system Model SE880 comprising Model SE881 workstation, colour monitor, VT100 compatible operating terminal and VDU, has achieved and largely exceeded design specifications. The system is able to acquire, archive and process survey data digitally in real time to a high degree of accuracy, producing quality displayed data. The system is compact, portable and easy to operate. It is able to operate both offshore and in the laboratory. As most software and operating processes are software based in 'C' operating on a VME bus architecture, this allows the system a great deal of flexibility. The system is therefore easily upgradeable in hardware and software, also it can be interfaced to other systems. Software and hardware from the system can be supplied to other compatible systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
